summary:
The sky looks still—until you press play. 
SkyShift X turns SPHEREx archive images into interactive sky movies, making the changing infrared universe accessible to everyone. Users enter sky coordinates, choose a field of view, and explore observations across dates and wavelengths. Images are aligned on a shared sky-coordinate grid and played chronologically, helping reveal possible movement and brightness changes. Wavelength controls distinguish spectral differences from changes over time.

Two modes welcome different explorers:
Beginner Mode offers simple controls and guided explanations for people with little astronomy knowledge. Research Mode provides deeper access to comparison tools, measurements, quality flags, and observation metadata to investigate candidate changes.

An integrated narrator with captions explains the images and evidence behind highlighted changes. Interactive 3D storytelling introduces SPHEREx and its mission without requiring prior astronomy knowledge.

Our solution addresses the challenge by transforming separate scientific observations into an intuitive visual experience. SkyShift X helps people watch, explore, and understand—connecting NASA’s open data with public curiosity, classroom learning, and deeper scientific investigation.
details:
The sky looks still—until you press play. 🛰️

SkyShift X turns real SPHEREx archive observations into interactive sky movies, bringing beginners and researchers into the same exploration—with different levels of detail.

Explore a place in the sky

The Sky Navigator offers coordinate entry, name search, and featured targets. Visitors can select a field of view and explore cases including Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

Or they can point coordinates on the map and the engine will search it easily

Watch observations become a movie

The viewer plays aligned infrared observations chronologically, with dates, wavelength information, adjustable speed, frame stepping, zoom, and a thumbnail timeline. Users can watch every observation or alternate between the first and last dates to make movement easier to notice.

These movies contain separate observations taken across time—not continuous spacecraft video.

Two modes, one set of observations

  • Beginner Mode provides a simple viewing experience and a “Can you find it?” interaction. Visitors can investigate independently or choose “Just show me” to reveal the measured change.
  • Research Mode adds wavelength and date controls, blink and comparison views, difference images, stacking tools, catalog overlays, spectra, quality flags, and detailed measurements with uncertainties.

A narrator tells the story behind the images

Narrated explanations with synchronized captions connect the observation sequence to its findings. They explain where we are looking, highlight measured changes, and summarize what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain. The interpretation comes from measurements and structured explanation templates; the voice presents that story.

Understand the mission through interactive exploration

The Universe Explorer provides educational experiences about SPHEREx when click MEET SphereX, the solar system, and the search for hypothetical distant worlds. These illustrations are distinguished from real observations, with a 2D fallback when 3D graphics are unavailable.

Know the telescope more

We understood that SPHEREx’s mission extends beyond Planet X:

it maps the infrared sky to study galaxies, cosmic history, and interstellar ice. Our interactive 3D explorer translates that broader mission into an accessible learning experience, connecting scientific context with real sky observations.

Why it matters

SkyShift X makes scientific images easier to access, compare, and understand. Beginners receive context, while researchers and experienced enthusiasts can inspect the supporting evidence.

The published demo includes clearly labeled saved movies built from real IRSA observations. Live retrieval and refreshing require the scientific backend. Throughout the experience, candidate changes are presented as findings to investigate—not automatic claims of discovery.
